name: Barn Quilt Trail
character: Barn quilts, back roads, and a map worth driving: golden prairie palette, big friendly signage type, volunteer-painted blocks.

sections.eyebrow: A driving trail of painted barn quilts
sections.title: {{guild_name}}
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Forty-one eight-foot blocks across four counties, painted by volunteers and hung where the corn can see them.

sections.heading: Plan a day on the trail

items.title: The full loop
items.body: Ninety miles, about six hours with stops. Two segments are gravel; the map says where.

items.title: The season
items.body: Blocks read best April through October, and the morning light is kindest to the paint.

items.title: Stop-and-shop farms
items.body: Five farms sell eggs, honey, and small quilts at the gate. Bring cash and a cooler.

items.title: Photo points
items.body: The map marks three pull-offs wide enough to stop safely. Please keep it to those.

sections.title: Paint the next block
sections.body: Membership funds paint, primer, and the bucket-truck rental. Members vote on the next routes.

sections.title: The trail
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Maps, gravel warnings, and where the pavement ends. Take the brochure; the barns do not have addresses.

sections.heading: How the trail works
sections.html:
Every block is numbered and named for its farm or its painter. The brochure groups them by county color so a wrong turn becomes a different loop instead of a lost afternoon. Printed maps live at the visitor center, the grain elevator office, and the diner on Route 24.

The trail is on working farms. Stay at the road, close the gate you opened, and wave; most farmers wave back and a few come out to talk about the pattern.

items.title: The north loop
items.body: Thirty-eight miles and fourteen blocks, mostly pavement, one covered bridge.

items.title: The river loop
items.body: Fifty-four miles along the bottom roads. Watch for combines in September.

items.title: The town loop
items.body: Twelve blocks in town, walkable in an afternoon, ends at the quilt shop.

sections.heading: Visitor center
sections.note: Free maps, cold water, and the volunteer who painted block 17 is usually around on Saturdays.

sections.title: Forty-one blocks and counting
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Each block names its farm, its pattern, and the volunteer who painted it.

items.title: Blazing Star, Hoxie farm
items.body: Block 1 and the reason the trail exists. Painted on the barn door, visible from half a mile.

items.title: Churn Dash, the grange hall
items.body: The only block on a public building, and the easiest photo stop on the trail.

items.title: Mariner's Compass, church camp
items.body: Painted by the confirmation class of 2022, eight feet of perfect points.

items.title: Flying Geese, Kessler dairy
items.body: Best seen at dusk, when the geese on the pond under it line up with the block.

items.title: Log Cabin, the old schoolhouse
items.body: Built from lumber salvaged out of the gym floor when the school consolidated. The block went up in 2021.

items.title: Honeybee, the apiary
items.body: Stop inside for honey. The block was the beekeeper's first attempt at geometry.

sections.label: Host a block on your barn

sections.title: Join the trail association
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Thirty dollars a year, a member's yard sign, and a vote on the next route.

sections.heading: What dues do
sections.html: Dues buy exterior paint, primer, the bucket-truck rental two weekends a year, and the brochure printing. The association is all volunteers; nobody has ever been paid, though the paint crew eats well at the fish fry.

items.a: Members, the 4-H club, and anyone who shows up to a paint day. Stencils and pattern help come free with the lumber.

items.q: How does a barn get picked?
items.a: Members nominate sites, the property owner signs an agreement, and the route vote decides which nominations are next.
Yes. Business members are listed on the map legend and get a small block for the storefront.

sections.title: About {{guild_name}}
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Started with a community-education class, four sheets of plywood, and more pattern books than sense.

sections.heading: From one class to four counties
sections.html:
The first block went up on the Hoxie farm in 2019 after a library class on barn quilts ran out of chairs. Neighbors asked for blocks of their own faster than the class could paint them, so the class became an association.

Now the trail keeps a MapGallery of finished blocks, a lumber stash behind the grange hall, and a waiting list that moves in the order the routes were voted. The paint is donated by the hardware store, which has never once let us pay.

items.quote: We drove the river loop on our anniversary. Somewhere around block 33 we started planning which barn we would hang one on.
items.author: Visitors from Topeka

sections.title: Contact the association
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Route suggestions, press requests, tour buses with questions, and landowners curious about a block.

sections.heading: Tour operators
sections.html: Bus groups are welcome on the paved loops. Write two weeks ahead and a volunteer meets the bus at the grange hall with maps and, if the season is right, honey.
